transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-10
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Sanjay Patel (Redwood AE), Laura Kim (Redwood SE), Ellen Cho (Meridian Head ML), Tom Alvarez (Infra), Priya Nair (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-gen - may be incomplete):
- Deep technical dive on autoscaling, burst tolerance, and reserved GPU sizing for Meridian's LLM inference workloads.
- Focus areas: queueing/backpressure model, KV-cache warmup strategies, batching tradeoffs, quantization impact and VPC/on-prem constraints.
- Agreed next steps: share burst simulation sheet; run a KV cache warmup benchmark on reserved A100s; Meridian to send token distribution and SLOs.

[00:00] Sanjay: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, uh quick roll call then we'll dive into the numbers.
[00:08] Ellen: hi, thanks, Ellen here.
[00:10] Tom: Tom, infra.
[00:12] Priya: Priya, security.
[00:14] Laura: Laura from Redwood, i'll start with a short context then we'll go deep.

[02:15] Laura: quick context — Meridian's wanting to run a customer-facing chat assistant and a reranking pipeline behind search, so the workload shapes are mixed: short chat sessions with many small prompts and a daily rerank batch that spikes. you told us there are two reserved A100s in prod and an auto-scale pool in staging?
[02:30] Ellen: yeah, prod is 2xA100 reserved, staging is an elastic pool third-party, but we can't rely on it for SLAs. major ask is to keep 95th < 300ms for chat generation and cost target under $0.0009/token average — and we want predictable degradation rather than hard failures.
[02:48] Laura: good that's helpful — so today's goal is to validate whether the reserved pool plus burst policy can hit those SLOs and how queueing/backpressure should behave.

[05:00] Tom: one quick infra note, we run inside a VPC on-prem colo and egress is restricted. we also have HSM-backed keys so any KMS talk needs to consider that flow.
[05:20] Priya: and SOC 2 plus some European data residency for a subset — might be relevant for where we route bursts.

[07:10] Sanjay: ok, jumping into the numbers — Laura, can you walk through the burst-sim sheet?
[07:18] Laura: yes, so baseline: model is a 13B decoder, avg prompt length 28 tokens, avg generated tokens 64, but tail events produce 10x request rate for 3-7 minutes. we modeled three configs: strict reserved only (2xA100), reserved + burst queue to a transient pool (hot-burst), and reserved + graceful degradation (quantized fallback on same nodes). the sim shows the reserved-only hits 95th at 420ms under 8x baseline load, so misses SLO. with a hot-burst ephemeral pool the 95th drops to 280ms but cost goes up about 22%.
[08:05] Tom: how are you modeling KV-cache warmup there? we saw big latency on cold starts.
[08:12] Laura: good call — the sim currently assumes no cache is warm for new conversations. we did a second pass that includes prefix caching with a 60% hit after 15s and that cuts CPU per token and latency by about 12% in the model. but that warmup time matters for short-lived chat sessions.
[08:34] Ellen: hm so for short chat sessions caching doesn't help much unless we pre-warm with synthetic traffic?
[08:40] Laura: yeah, exactly. options: 1) synthetic warmers (cheap but adds extra tokens), 2) prefetch top-k KV entries for high-frequency prompts, 3) accept higher 95th on cold sessions. we recommend hybrid: targeted prefetch + short-lived synthetic bursts during predictable windows.

[10:05] Priya: from security — any synthetic warming traffic stored or logged? we need to ensure it doesn't persist or leak.
[10:12] Laura: synthetic warmers can be configured as non-persistent and excluded from logs; Redwood's private deployments can mark those tokens and skip retention. we'll add that to the security doc.

[12:20] Sanjay: let's talk queueing/backpressure model — we prefer something that keeps tail latency bounded and avoids OOM or request loss.
[12:30] Laura: our proposal is a three-tier queueing policy: immediate exec queue (reserved), overflow queue with controlled concurrency and token-based prioritization, and a longer-duration deferred queue that returns 429s before reaching system limits. that lets you surface graceful degradation (e.g., shorter generations) for lower priority users.
[12:58] Tom: token-based prioritization? can you explain?
[13:05] Laura: yes — requests get a token-cost estimate at arrival (prompt+expected generation). we prioritize lower-cost items to maximize throughput under fixed GPU memory/compute; also supports throttling long-form jobs into the deferred queue. the sim shows this improves 95th by 6-9% under medium load.

[15:00] Ellen: curious about bursting to private nodes — we can't use public hosted ephemeral due to data residency, can Redwood burst to our on-prem capacity or a partner region?
[15:10] Sanjay: yes — Redwood Private supports routing to customer-managed nodes in the same VPC/on-prem or to a partner region. there are tradeoffs: network egress and extra latency from routing, plus capacity planning on the customer's side.
[15:28] Tom: what about cold-KV across regions? cross-region KV sync is slow.
[15:33] Laura: cross-region is rough; for cold KV we recommend replicating hot KV shards locally or using a cachestamp with pre-warm snapshots. another pattern: a tiny local cache with a higher miss penalty to the central store — keeps tail lower.

[17:40] Priya: quantization — if we use 8-bit or 4-bit to save memory, how does that change latency and quality?
[17:48] Laura: quantization reduces memory footprint and can allow higher concurrency, which reduces per-token latency on average, but there's model quality risk depending on the model family. our testing with the customer's selected 13B shows 8-bit QAT-style yields negligible quality drop, 4-bit anecdotally has a 3-6% regression on reranking accuracy. we can do a targeted eval with your rerank dataset.
[18:20] Tom: and does quantization affect KV cache formats?
[18:24] Laura: not directly; KV cache is raw hidden states — quantizing the model doesn't change cache shape but may change token outputs, so caching still helps. cache storage can be compressed separately.

[20:05] Sanjay: discuss reserved GPU sizing — you have 2xA100 today; sim suggests 3xA100 would meet SLOs without burst but flows cost up ~35%. cheaper option is keep 2xA100 and add a small hot-burst of 1xA40 or T4-like for short tail events. that reduces cost increase to ~12% while hitting 95th ~290ms in sim.
[20:40] Ellen: A40/T4 have lower FP throughput and may increase latency for long sequences, right?
[20:45] Laura: yes for long sequences they'd be slower; but for short chat bursts they might be okay because of higher concurrency and lower cost — it's about matching your tail profile. we can simulate mixed-node pools.

[22:30] Tom: on autoscaler behavior — if we spin up ephemeral nodes during bursts, how do we ensure model load time and KV warmup doesn't negate benefits?
[22:38] Laura: great question — this is the warmup problem. Redwoods' hot-burst flow supports two techniques: snapshot-based model load (fast load using precompiled bits) and KV prefetch from snapshots so new nodes start with a warmed cache subset. combined these reduce effective cold-start penalty to ~8-18s in our tests; cold without snapshots can be 40-90s.

[24:00] Ellen: 8-18s still seems high for a 3-5 minute spike.
[24:06] Laura: true — so we recommend one of the following: 1) keep a minimal standby instance ready (adds steady-state cost), 2) use pre-warm windows (schedule short spin-ups when you expect traffic), or 3) accept higher 95th and use prioritized queuing to hide the worst tails. most customers pick hybrid: 1 standby + small ephemeral bursts.

[26:30] Sanjay: let's probe the queue depth and backpressure numbers — what does the sim use for service time distributions?
[26:35] Laura: we used empirical traces you provided for the first 90 days; fitted a log-normal for service times and a non-homogenous Poisson process for arrivals with burst spikes. queue capacity was tuned to bound queueing delay under 99th percentile for most scenarios.
[27:10] Tom: any risk of OOM if we allow large batch sizes?
[27:14] Laura: yes — batch size is a tradeoff: larger batch -> better GPU throughput but increased queuing and memory pressure. we recommend dynamic batching with an upper memory-based cap; the runtime tracks kv cache occupancy and will reduce batch size proactively when mem approaches threshold. this avoids OOM but can increase dispatch frequency.

[29:00] Priya: auditing and logs during bursts — how we maintain traceability?
[29:05] Sanjay: Redwood Console keeps per-request tracing and marks burst-sourced traffic; logs can be filtered to exclude synthetic warmers; audit trails for model loads and node spin-ups are retained for 90 days by default in Private. we can extend retention.

[31:40] Laura: i want to call out an edge case we found: if many short sessions hit the system simultaneously, KV misses spike and cause a synchronous increase in GPU compute due to retrieval overhead leading to a feedback loop. mitigation is to add a small request coalescer that groups similar early requests and warms a shared prefix, or to favor prefetch for top-k prompts.
[32:05] Ellen: do you have numbers on how the coalescer impacts user-perceived latency?
[32:10] Laura: yes — in our tests coalescing reduced 95th by ~14% on short-session-heavy workloads with negligible impact on median.

[34:00] Tom: about the quantization fallback — if we automatically switch to q4 or q8 during bursts, how do we validate output quality? we can't have silent regressions.
[34:10] Laura: Redwood's rollout supports canarying and eval hooks — you can run a subset of queries through the quantized model and compare rerank scores or LM logprobs. Laura: also you can set automatic rollback thresholds (e.g., 2% drop in rerank NDCG triggers rollback). we'll help set up the eval harness against your datasets.

[36:20] Priya: network — if we route to partner region under burst, what's the latency impact?
[36:25] Laura: depends on geography — for NA->EU partner it was 60-110ms added in our experiments. that's sometimes acceptable for non-interactive rerank, not for chat. routing policies can be per-route.

[38:10] Ellen: pricing clarity — if we use hot-burst ephemeral with pre-warm snapshots, what line items change?
[38:18] Sanjay: main differences: reserved monthly fee unchanged; ephemeral burst is billed on a per-minute basis plus model load snapshot storage; snapshot storage is small relative but counts. we'll include a modeled cost breakdown in the sheet we share.

[40:00] Laura: operationally, recommended config for us to hit your SLOs with reasonable cost: keep 2xA100 reserved, add 1 standby warm node (half-resourced) and a hot-burst pool of 1xA40 with snapshot pre-warm. prioritize KV prefetch for top-200 prompts and enable dynamic batching with memory-aware caps.
[40:28] Ellen: sounds reasonable — what about progressive rollouts if we change model or quantization?
[40:33] Sanjay: Redwood supports canary deploys per route and automatic rollback on metric regression; we can tie rollback to rerank evals and latency SLOs.

[42:15] Tom: can you run one realistic benchmark with our exact token distribution and the 2xA100 + A40 hot-burst config? we'd like to see p50/p95/p99 plus cost delta.
[42:24] Laura: yes — that's part of Laura's action item. we'll need the token distribution and a playback harness.

[44:50] Ellen: on the security side, we need a note on HSM key flow when snapshotting models and caches.
[44:56] Priya: yes the snapshot should not leak keys and KMS calls should remain inside customer VPC.
[45:02] Sanjay: agreed — we'll annotate the security doc and add an architecture diagram for HSM/KMS flow.

[47:20] (brief crosstalk)
[47:36] Laura: quick real-world anecdote: a retail customer used a small standby + aggressive coalescer and reduced tail by 37% without more than 10% cost increase. so hybrid patterns work in practice.

[50:00] Ellen: ok recap pls — what are the concrete next steps?
[50:05] Sanjay: recap: 1) Redwood to share burst simulation workbook and detailed cost model (Sanjay) by 2/13. 2) Redwood to run KV-cache warmup benchmark using Meridian's token distribution on 2xA100 + A40 hot-burst and share logs (Laura) by 2/20. 3) Meridian to send token distribution and target SLOs (Ellen) by 2/12. 4) Redwood to update security doc re: synthetic warmers and HSM flow (Sanjay) by 2/16.
[50:42] Priya: i'll expect the security doc updates and will review.
[51:00] Tom: we'll also share production traces and a playback harness artifact.

[55:00] Sanjay: any other concerns or open questions?
[55:05] Ellen: can you include an option that explores compressing KV cache to save memory?
[55:10] Laura: yes we'll add an option — compression tradeoff is CPU vs RAM. we'll add numbers.

[58:00] (wrap-up)
[58:10] Sanjay: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the sheet and a scheduled benchmark slot.
[58:20] Ellen: thanks.
[58:22] Tom: thanks all.
[58:25] Priya: bye.
